rows.solution:
\(\sin 4\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sin 60^\circ\), so \(4\theta = 60^\circ\) and \(\theta = 15^\circ\).

Then \(\dfrac{\theta}{3} = 5^\circ\), which is option (D) \(5^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.solution:
Multiply by 3 to clear the fractions: \(3p(y) = 21y^2 - 11y - 2 = 21y^2 - 14y + 3y - 2 = 7y(3y - 2) + (3y - 2) = (3y - 2)(7y + 1)\).

So the zeroes are \(y = \dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(y = -\dfrac{1}{7}\), which is option (D) \(\dfrac{2}{3}, -\dfrac{1}{7}\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: A system of two linear equations in two variables is inconsistent, if the lines in the graph are :
rows.solution:
An inconsistent system has no solution, so its two lines never meet. Two distinct lines in a plane that never meet are parallel.

This is option (B) parallel.

\(\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} = \sqrt{\sin^2\theta} = \sin\theta\) (for an acute angle \(\theta\), where \(\sin\theta > 0\)).

So \(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta}} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \cot\theta\), which is option (A) \(\cot\theta\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: The discriminant of the quadratic equation \(bx^2 + ax + c = 0;\ b \neq 0\) is given by :
rows.solution:
For \(Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0\) the discriminant is \(B^2 - 4AC\). Here the coefficient of \(x^2\) is b, the coefficient of x is a and the constant term is c.

So the discriminant is \(a^2 - 4bc\), which is option (D) \(a^2 - 4bc\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: If the mid-point of the line segment joining the points \((a, 4)\) and \((2, 2b)\) is \((2, 6)\), then the value of \((a + b)\) is given by :
rows.solution:
The mid-point of \((a, 4)\) and \((2, 2b)\) is \(\left(\dfrac{a + 2}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 2b}{2}\right) = (2, 6)\).

\(\dfrac{a + 2}{2} = 2\) gives \(a = 2\), and \(\dfrac{4 + 2b}{2} = 6\) gives \(b = 4\).

So \(a + b = 6\), which is option (A) \(6\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If the sum of the zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x) = (p + 1)x^2 + (2p + 3)x + (3p + 4)\) is \(-1\), then find the value of ‘p’.
rows.solution:
For \(p(x) = (p + 1)x^2 + (2p + 3)x + (3p + 4)\), the sum of the zeroes is \(-\dfrac{2p + 3}{p + 1}\).

\(-\dfrac{2p + 3}{p + 1} = -1\), so \(2p + 3 = p + 1\) and \(p = -2\).

(Then \(p + 1 = -1 \neq 0\), so the polynomial is still quadratic.)

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 - 2x - 1\), then find the value of \(\dfrac{1}{2\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{2\beta} + 3\alpha\beta\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(\left(4\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{5}{3}\right)\) is an irrational number given that \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(4\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{5}{3}\) is rational, equal to \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) with a and b integers and \(b \neq 0\).

Then \(4\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{a}{b} - \dfrac{5}{3} = \dfrac{3a - 5b}{3b}\), so \(\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{3a - 5b}{12b}\).

Since \(3a - 5b\) and \(12b\) are integers with \(12b \neq 0\), the right side is rational. That would make \(\sqrt{2}\) rational, contradicting the given fact that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

So \(4\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{5}{3}\) is irrational.

rows.stem:
If 65% of the population has black eyes, 25% have brown eyes and the remaining have blue eyes, what is the probability that a person selected at random has :

(a) blue eyes ?

(b) brown or black eyes ?
rows.solution:
The share with blue eyes is \(100\% - 65\% - 25\% = 10\%\).

(a) \(P(\text{blue eyes}) = \dfrac{10}{100} = \dfrac{1}{10}\).

(b) Brown or black eyes covers \(65\% + 25\% = 90\%\), so \(P(\text{brown or black eyes}) = \dfrac{90}{100} = \dfrac{9}{10}\).

(Equivalently, it is the complement of blue eyes: \(1 - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{9}{10}\).)

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: An AP consists of ‘n’ terms whose \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is 4 and the common difference is 2. If the sum of ‘n’ terms of AP is \(-14\), then find ‘n’. Also, find the sum of the first 20 terms.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a. The common difference is \(d = 2\).

The nth term is 4: \(a + (n - 1) \times 2 = 4\), so \(a + 2n = 6\) and \(a = 6 - 2n\).

The sum of the n terms is \(-14\): \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n - 1) \times 2\right] = -14\), that is \(n(a + n - 1) = -14\).

Substituting \(a = 6 - 2n\): \(n(6 - 2n + n - 1) = -14\), so \(n(5 - n) = -14\), that is \(n^2 - 5n - 14 = 0\).

\((n - 7)(n + 2) = 0\), and since n is a number of terms, \(n = 7\). Then \(a = 6 - 14 = -8\).

(Check: the AP \(-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4\) has 7 terms, last term 4, and sum \(\dfrac{7}{2}(-8 + 4) = -14\).)

\(S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}\left[2 \times (-8) + 19 \times 2\right] = 10(-16 + 38) = 220\).

So \(n = 7\) and the sum of the first 20 terms is 220.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The sum of the first six terms of an arithmetic progression is 42. The ratio of the \(10^{\text{th}}\) term to the \(30^{\text{th}}\) term is 1 : 3. Calculate the first and the thirteenth terms of the AP.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a and the common difference d.

\(\dfrac{a_{10}}{a_{30}} = \dfrac{a + 9d}{a + 29d} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(3a + 27d = a + 29d\), giving \(2a = 2d\) and \(a = d\).

\(S_6 = \dfrac{6}{2}\left[2a + 5d\right] = 42\). With \(d = a\): \(3 \times 7a = 42\), so \(a = 2\) and \(d = 2\).

\(a_{13} = a + 12d = 2 + 12 \times 2 = 26\).

So the first term is 2 and the thirteenth term is 26. (Check: \(a_{10} = 20\) and \(a_{30} = 60\), in the ratio \(1 : 3\).)

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: A man lent a part of his money at 10% p.a. and the rest at 15% p.a. His income at the end of the year is ₹ 1,900. If he had interchanged the rate of interest on the two sums, he would have earned ₹ 200 more. Find the amount lent in both cases.
rows.solution:
Let ₹ \(x\) be lent at 10% p.a. and ₹ \(y\) at 15% p.a.

The year's income is ₹ 1,900: \(\dfrac{10x}{100} + \dfrac{15y}{100} = 1900\), that is \(2x + 3y = 38000\) ... (i)

With the rates interchanged he would earn ₹ \(1900 + 200 = 2100\): \(\dfrac{15x}{100} + \dfrac{10y}{100} = 2100\), that is \(3x + 2y = 42000\) ... (ii)

Adding (i) and (ii): \(5x + 5y = 80000\), so \(x + y = 16000\) ... (iii)

Subtracting (i) from (ii): \(x - y = 4000\) ... (iv)

From (iii) and (iv): \(2x = 20000\), so \(x = 10000\) and \(y = 6000\).

(Check: \(1000 + 900 = 1900\), and with the rates swapped \(1500 + 600 = 2100\).)

So ₹ 10,000 was lent at 10% p.a. and ₹ 6,000 at 15% p.a.
